newsitem.title: USA: US Senators seek to close stock option loophole.
newsitem.headline: US Senators seek to close stock option loophole.

text.p: Sens. Carl Levin and John McCain said Tuesday they will seek to require companies to report stock options paid to executives as expenses in shareholders' reports if they want to take income tax deductions for the options as payments to executives.

Levin, a Michigan Democrat, said it would not bar stock options but would require equal treatment under tax law and in accounting to the public. McCain, an Arizona Republican, said, "If companies choose not to fully disclose how much they're compensating their executives, they certainly shouldn't be able to claim a tax benefit from it."

Levin, in a telephone conference call with reporters, said that if his bill were enacted into law, companies would still be free to avoid reporting stock options as expenses in reports to shareholders. However, if they did so, they could not also take tax deductions for the options as corporate expenses.

"There is a broad feeling that something is out of whack in this area," on chief executive pay, Levin said. He said there is a growing sentiment that the gap between worker and executive pay is too large, but Congress has been reluctant to take any action to legislate pay.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated the government would gain $933 million over the next 10 years from companies electing to forego the tax deduction in order to legally avoid showing the stock options as compensationexpenses on their books.
"It is clear CEO's have fought very hard to keep this form of compensation off their books," Levin said.
